answer_text:
Assume the integral is taken in the usual Lebesgue sense, so \(E\) is measurable. Let

\[
A=\int_E e^{it}\,dt .
\]

If \(A=0\), there is nothing to prove. Otherwise, choose \(\theta\) such that \(e^{i\theta}=A/|A|\). Then

\[
|A|=\operatorname{Re}\!\left(e^{-i\theta}A\right)
=\operatorname{Re}\!\left(e^{-i\theta}\int_E e^{it}\,dt\right)
=\int_E \cos(t-\theta)\,dt.
\]

For any fixed \(\theta\),

\[
\cos(t-\theta)\le (\cos(t-\theta))_+,
\]

where \((x)_+=\max\{x,0\}\). Hence

\[
|A|\le \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} (\cos(t-\theta))_+\,dt.
\]

The function \((\cos(t-\theta))_+\) is \(2\pi\)-periodic, so its integral over any full interval of length \(2\pi\) is the same as over one positive half-wave:

\[
\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} (\cos(t-\theta))_+\,dt
=
\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \cos u\,du
=
\sin u\Big|_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}
=2.
\]

Thus

\[
\left|\int_E e^{it}\,dt\right|\le 2
\]

for every measurable \(E\subset[-\pi,\pi)\).

This bound is sharp. Take

\[
E=\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right).
\]

Then

\[
\int_E e^{it}\,dt
=
\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} e^{it}\,dt
=
\frac{e^{it}}{i}\Bigg|_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}
=
\frac{i-(-i)}{i}
=
2.
\]

Therefore the supremum is actually attained and equals

\[
\boxed{2}.
\]
